name: free-audio-clap-zig
description: Handmade Zig bindings to CLAP ABI
readme_content:
free-audio-clap-zig

Handmade Zig bindings to free-audio's CLAP ABI.

Supported Versions

  • clap-1.2.7 zig master

After Zig 0.16.0 this package will actively support the latest release and master branch.

The CLAP version will be whatever is current. In the unlikely event of a breaking API change, this package will only support the new version.

Differences from original

Adapted the namespacing to be more "Zig-like". See API Changes.

These bindings avoid redundant naming. So intead of clap.factory.PluginFactory we use clap.Plugin.Factory.

Usage

Fetch

Use zig fetch to add this package to your dependency list.

This will use the latest CLAP version and Zig's master branch.

zig fetch --save git+https://codeberg.org/sonro/free-audio-clap-zig.git

Build

Add to your build.zig. See basic example for more detail.

const clap_zig = b.dependency("free_audio_clap_zig", .{});
plugin_module.addImport("clap", clap_zig.module("clap-zig"));

Use

In the root of your plugin module:

const clap = @import("clap");

pub export const clap_entry = clap.Entry{
    .init = entryInit,
    .deinit = entryDeinit,
    .getFactory = entryGetFactory,
};

fn entryInit(_: clap.CStr) callconv(.c) bool {
    return true;
}
...

Examples

Check out the examples folder for more in-depth usage. Use zig build examples to create the example plugins.

Other bindings

There are 2 other Zig bindings I've found, but they either lack documentation or don't target the latest Zig/CLAP versions.

  • interpunct/clap-zig-bindings
  • jsfer/jam_clap

name: zls
description:
Stateless link shortener inspired by ha.mr.

https://zillowe.qzz.io/docs/zds/zls
readme_content:
ZLS

Zillowe Link Shortener

Stateless link shortener inspired by [`ha.mr`](https://github.com/p2r3/ha.mr).


How it works

ZLS uses a stateless compression engine written in Zig and compiled to WebAssembly. Unlike traditional shorteners (like Bitly), ZLS does not use a database. Instead, it compresses the destination URL into a high-density Base84 string and stores it directly in the URL fragment (after the #).

When a user visits a ZLS link, the frontend loads the WASM module, decompresses the payload, and performs an instantaneous client-side redirect.

Key Features

  • Zero Database: Permanent links with zero maintenance cost.
  • Privacy First: No tracking, no logs, no middleman.
  • High Performance: Heavy lifting handled by Zig at near-native speeds in the browser.
  • Static Hosting: Can be hosted anywhere (GitHub Pages, GitLab Pages, Vercel).

Architecture

  • src/: Core compression engine (Zig).
  • app/: Web application (TypeScript/Hono).
  • docs/: Documentation (Fumadocs).

Installation

You can install the ZLS binary using Zoi:

zoi install @zillowe/zls

Development

Prerequisites

  • Zig 0.16.0
  • Deno
  • Just

Setup

  1. Build the WASM module:

    just wasm

  2. Run the development server:

    just start

  3. Open http://localhost:8000 in your browser.

Deployment (GitLab Pages)

ZLS is designed to be hosted as a static site. The CI/CD pipeline (.gitlab-ci.yml) builds the Zig WASM and bundles the frontend into the public/ directory for hosting.

name: ZVC
description: Simple Script for Zig Version Control written shell(POSIX-sh)
readme_content:
ZVC - Zig Version Control

Tool sederhana untuk menginstall, mengelola, dan menggunakan berbagai versi Zig di sistem Linux dan macOS. Dibuat murni menggunakan POSIX sh - tanpa dependency tambahan selain curl atau wget dan tar.

sudo zvc -i 0.16.0
sudo zvc -s 0.16.0
zig version

Fitur

  • Install beberapa versi Zig secara bersamaan
  • Deteksi arsitektur dan OS otomatis
  • Support binary, source code, dan bootstrap tarball
  • Support versi nightly (master)
  • Set versi default sistem
  • Gunakan versi tertentu secara sementara (per-session)
  • Remove per-versi, per-variant, atau semua sekaligus
  • Portabel: berjalan di semua arsitektur dan libc (glibc/musl)
  • Tidak memerlukan Rust, Python, Node.js, atau runtime lainnya

Dependency

Dependency Keterangan
sh POSIX sh (dash, bash, busybox sh, dll)
curl atau wget Salah satu wajib tersedia
tar Untuk ekstraksi tarball

Instalasi

git clone https://github.com/gh0st4n/ZVC
cd ZVC
sudo sh install.sh

Verifikasi:

zvc -v

Untuk menghapus ZVC dari sistem:

sudo sh uninstall.sh

Penggunaan

Install Zig

Install versi stabil — arch terdeteksi otomatis:

sudo zvc -i 0.16.0

Tentukan arch secara manual:

sudo zvc -i 0.16.0 aarch64

Install source code atau bootstrap:

sudo zvc -i 0.16.0 source
sudo zvc -i 0.16.0 bootstrap

Install versi nightly (master):

sudo zvc -i master
sudo zvc -i master source
sudo zvc -i master bootstrap

Lihat Daftar Versi

Versi yang tersedia di ziglang.org:

zvc -l download

Output:

  VERSION      VARIANT        PLATFORM
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  master        source         All (Zig Source Code)
  master        bootstrap      All (Zig Bootstrap)
  master        x86_64         Linux / MacOS / Windows / FreeBSD / NetBSD / OpenBSD
  master        aarch64        Linux / MacOS / Windows / FreeBSD / NetBSD / OpenBSD
  ...

Versi yang sudah terinstall di sistem:

zvc -l system

Output:

  NAME                                     PATH
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0                 /opt/zvc/zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0
  zig-source-0.16.0                        /opt/zvc/zig-source-0.16.0

Set Versi Default

Menjadikan versi tertentu sebagai zig default di seluruh sistem (/usr/local/bin/zig):

sudo zvc -s 0.16.0
sudo zvc -s master

Verifikasi:

zig version

Hapus default tanpa uninstall Zig-nya:

sudo zvc -d

Gunakan Versi Tertentu (Sementara)

Aktifkan versi tertentu hanya untuk session terminal saat ini:

zvc -u 0.16.0
zvc -u master

Langsung jalankan perintah Zig dengan versi tertentu:

zvc -u 0.16.0 -- build
zvc -u 0.16.0 -- version
zvc -u master -- build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe

Tentukan arch secara manual:

zvc -u 0.16.0 x86_64 -- build

Remove Zig

Hapus semua Zig yang terinstall:

sudo zvc -r all

Hapus semua variant dari satu versi:

sudo zvc -r 0.16.0
sudo zvc -r master
sudo zvc -r source
sudo zvc -r bootstrap

Hapus satu variant spesifik:

sudo zvc -r 0.16.0 x86_64
sudo zvc -r 0.16.0 source
sudo zvc -r 0.16.0 bootstrap

Struktur Direktori

/opt/zvc/
├── zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0/        ← binary (x86_64, Linux, stable)
│   ├── zig
│   ├── lib/
│   └── ...
├── zig-aarch64-linux-0.16.0/       ← binary (aarch64, Linux, stable)
├── zig-source-0.16.0/              ← source code tarball
├── zig-bootstrap-0.16.0/           ← bootstrap tarball
└── zig-x86_64-linux-0.17.0-dev.956+2dca73595/  ← master/nightly

Arsitektur yang Didukung

uname -m Target Zig OS
x86_64 x86_64 Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD
aarch64 aarch64 Linux, macOS, Windows, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD
armv7l, armv6l arm Linux, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD
riscv64 riscv64 Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD
i386, i686 x86 Linux, Windows, NetBSD
loongarch64 loongarch64 Linux
s390x s390x Linux

Referensi Perintah

sudo zvc -i, --install <version> [arch]      Install Zig
zvc  -l, --list [download|system]            Tampilkan daftar Zig
sudo zvc -r, --remove <version|all> [arch]   Hapus Zig
zvc  -u, --use <version> [arch] [-- ...]     Gunakan versi tertentu (sementara)
sudo zvc -s, --set <version> [arch]          Set versi default sistem
sudo zvc -d, --disable                       Hapus symlink default
zvc  -h, --help                              Tampilkan bantuan
zvc  -v, --version                           Tampilkan versi ZVC

Catatan

  • source dan bootstrap tidak memiliki binary zig — keduanya digunakan untuk membangun Zig dari source, bukan untuk development langsung
  • Versi master ter-install dengan nama folder yang menyertakan full version string (misal: zig-x86_64-linux-0.17.0-dev.956+2dca73595)
  • Binary dari arsitektur berbeda tidak bisa dijalankan di mesin yang tidak kompatibel — ZVC akan memberikan error yang jelas
  • Setelah sudo zvc -d atau sudo zvc -r, jalankan hash -r atau buka terminal baru untuk membersihkan cache shell

Lisensi

MIT License — bebas digunakan, dimodifikasi, dan didistribusikan.

@T4n-Labs · @Gh0sT4n

name: advent-of-code
description: Solutions for Advent of Code problems
readme_content:
Advent of Code

This is my repository for my solutions to Advent of Code.

Usage

Get your session token from AoC and have an environment variable called AOC_SESSION in .env.

Use just get-all-inputs to download your input files, and if you're not me, then the tests will all fail, because they test against my real input.

Structure

Every year has a folder, which contains a folder for each language used for that year. Each language folder has a language-specific structure but every day should be in a separate folder. For example, 2025/zig/day-4 contains all the code for that day, and should compile on its own. Sometimes I write a shared library to use across multiple days, and those are handled differently by each language.

Every language folder should contain a flake.nix, flake.lock, .envrc, and justfile. The flake provides a development shell and nothing else, the justfile looks like

import "../../justfile"

set allow-duplicate-recipes

_default:
    @just --list

# check the current day
[group("check")]
[no-cd]
check:
    cargo nextest run
    cargo nextest run --release

# check every day this year
[group("check")]
check-year:
    set -e; for d in {{ source_directory() }}/day*; do cd "$d" && just check; done

and the .envrc looks like

nix_direnv_manual_reload
source_up
use flake

name: dyos
description: Hobby OS written in Zig targeting RISC-V
readme_content:
DyOS

This is my attempt to create a hobby operating system, written mostly in Zig and targeting RISC-V (at least for now).

Why the name?

My name is Dyson, and my naming scheme for this project is to slap a dy- prefix on most things, like init becomes dynit, the shell is dysh, etc. Having a consistent naming scheme solves one of the hardest problems of computer science. The other three of course being cache invalidation and off-by-one errors.

Why Zig?

Because it looks like a really powerful language and I want to learn it.

Why RISC-V?

Partly because it's simpler than x86 or ARM, but the assembly content in this project is sparse, so I'm using RISC-V mostly for fun. It's also one of the easiest architectures to emulate, so maybe someday I'll write my own emulator to run my own OS.

Then I can design my own implementation of RISC-V and print my own silicon to run my own OS. Then of course I'll have to design my own language with its own self-hosted compiler and port this whole project to my own language, and then I can finally live out my dreams of becoming a goose farmer.

name: turian
readme_content:
Turian Engine

A component-based 3D game engine and editor built entirely in Zig.

Turian gives you a Unity-style workflow — scene hierarchy, inspector, drag-and-drop asset management, and live script discovery — without the runtime overhead or licensing fees of commercial engines.

Website · Download · Docs · Discord · Matrix

Screenshots

Turian Studio — editor + viewport

Install

Download a binary release (recommended)

Download the latest SDK from the Releases page. You only need Zig 0.16.0 — nothing else.

# Linux / macOS
tar xf turian-sdk-linux-x86_64-v0.1.0.tar.gz
export PATH="$PWD/turian-sdk-linux-x86_64-v0.1.0:$PATH"

# Windows (PowerShell)
Expand-Archive turian-sdk-windows-x86_64-v0.1.0.zip
$env:Path += ";$PWD\turian-sdk-windows-x86_64-v0.1.0"

Then create your first project:

turian-cli new-project my-game "My Game"
turian-cli build       my-game

See the SDK guide for more details and the full CLI reference.

Build from source

git lfs install
git clone https://gitlab.com/mass4org/mega4/turian.git && cd turian
zig build run          # compile + launch the editor
zig build test         # run all tests

See docs/install.md for the full developer setup.

Why Turian?

Most engines force a trade-off: the productivity of a visual editor or the control of a low-level systems language. Turian refuses the trade.

  • One language, top to bottom. The engine, the editor, your game logic, and the build tooling are all Zig. No VM, no scripting bridge, no FFI tax.
  • No garbage collector, no hidden allocations. Your game ships as a single native executable with predictable performance.
  • Editor-first, but never locked in. Scenes are human-readable text you can diff and merge; the CLI builds the exact same game headlessly for CI.
  • Free as in freedom. MPLv2, no seats, no revenue share, no per-title fees.

Component scripting

// assets/spinner.zig
const engine = @import("engine");

pub const Spinner = struct {
    pub const is_component = true;

    speed: f32 = 90.0,   // degrees / second — editable in inspector

    pub fn update(self: *Spinner, time: engine.Time) void {
        _ = self.speed * time.delta;
    }
};

Drop spinner.zig in your project's assets/ folder. Turian discovers it automatically on the next Refresh and lists it under Add Component ▾.

Documentation

Guide Description
Getting started Open a project, write a component, build a game
Install / build from source Developer setup
SDK guide Ship games without the engine checkout
ADRs Architecture decision records

Full documentation is at turian.mass4.org/docs.

Community

  • Discord — #turian channel
  • Matrix — #turian:matrix.org
  • Issues & MRs — GitLab

Contributions are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md.

Sponsorship

Turian is developed and maintained by Bruno Massa and contributors. If it saves you time or money, consider supporting the project:

License

Turian is free software, licensed under the MPL v2. Copyright © 2026 Bruno Massa.

name: zsm
description:
Modern, security-first replacement for bash-based installation scripts

https://zillowe.qzz.io/docs/zds/zsm
readme_content:
ZSM

Zillowe Script Manager

Modern, security-first replacement for bash-based installation scripts.


ZSM is a modern, security-first replacement for bash-based installation scripts.

The Problem

Running curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | bash is a common but dangerous pattern. It grants arbitrary, unvetted execution privileges to a remote script, often requiring sudo.

The ZSM Solution

ZSM introduces a Capability-based Security model for installation scripts. Instead of running imperative shell code, you run a .zsm script that declares the permissions it needs. ZSM acts as a complete lifecycle manager.

Key Features

  • Declarative Permissions: Scripts must explicitly request access to the network, filesystem, or system configuration.
  • Deep Supervision: Lock external binaries to specific argument patterns (e.g. require bin: curl --silent).
  • User Approval & Persistence: Users review and approve specific capabilities before any code runs. Approvals are securely cached based on the script's URL.
  • Full Lifecycle Management: ZSM tracks created files and supports zsm uninstall for clean removal, including custom uninstall hooks.
  • Small & Portable: Built with Zig 0.16.0 for zero-dependency, high-performance execution.

Installation

You can install ZSM via Zoi:

zoi install @zillowe/zsm

Usage

ZSM can fetch and run scripts natively or via pipes:

# Native execution (Recommended)
zsm install https://example.com/install.zsm

# Piped execution
curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.zsm | zsm

Script Example (install.zsm)

ZSM scripts use a declarative format to specify metadata and requirements, followed by safe built-in logic:

#!/usr/bin/env zsm
# :: name: my-app
# :: version: 1.0.0
# :: require bin: gpg, tar
# :: perm net: example.com
# :: perm fs: ~/.local/bin

LATEST_TAG = web.get_json_field("https://example.com/api/latest", "tag_name")
web.download("https://example.com/${LATEST_TAG}.tar.gz", "/tmp/app.tar.gz")

fs.move("/tmp/app", "~/.local/bin/app")

Development

To build ZSM from source:

zig build

To run tests:

zig build test

To install build ZSM latest version for Zoi as a .zpa archive run:

zoi package build ./zsm.pkg.lua

This will build the latest commit of ZSM, to install that archive run:

zoi package install ./zsm-*.zpa

ZSM is developed by Zusty < Zillowe Foundation
Part of the Zillowe Development Suite (ZDS)

name: open-asset-package
readme_content:
Open Asset Package (OAP)

A language-agnostic, streamable asset package format for games and applications — plus a zero-dependency Zig reference implementation.

An .oap file bundles many assets (textures, meshes, audio, scripts, scenes, arbitrary blobs) into a single container that supports:

  • Random access — any asset is located in O(log n) via a sorted index; the data section is never scanned.
  • Per-asset compression — store or deflate per blob, so one asset can be decompressed without touching the rest.
  • Per-asset encryption — optional xor (obfuscation) or chacha20 per blob; the key is supplied by the app and never stored in the package, so assets can't be casually extracted (deterrent, not DRM).
  • Stable content addressing — every asset has a 128-bit id (use UUIDs, hashes, whatever you like) plus an optional human-readable virtual path.
  • Streaming / partial loading — the header and index fully describe blob locations, so consumers can range-fetch individual assets (e.g. over HTTP) without downloading the whole package.
  • Patching / DLC / mods — ship a partial package containing only changed assets and mount it over a base package; the overlay's versions win and everything else falls through. See examples/.
  • Dependencies & manifests — assets can declare dependencies on other assets; packages carry a manifest describing themselves and the other packages they require (base game, DLC, patches, mods…).

The on-disk format is fully specified in SPEC.md and is free to implement by anyone, in any language.

Third-party implementations are welcome

OAP is meant to be an open, interoperable format — not a Zig-only library. The specification is deliberately small and unencumbered. If you want a reader or writer in C, Rust, Go, Python, JavaScript, C#, Swift, or anything else:

  1. Read SPEC.md — it is the normative, byte-level description.
  2. Follow the porting checklist in docs/implementing.md.
  3. Validate against the canonical package in testdata/sample.oap and its source files under testdata/sample/.

Specification, the Zig implementation, the CLI tooling, and the documentation are intentionally distributed together in this one repository so that an implementer has everything needed in a single place.

CLI

oap pack     <dir> <out.oap> [--name NAME] [--store]
oap unpack   <file.oap> <out-dir>
oap list     <file.oap>
oap inspect  <file.oap>
oap validate <file.oap>

zig build                       # builds zig-out/bin/oap
oap pack ./assets game.oap --name core
oap inspect game.oap
oap validate game.oap

pack walks a directory, storing each file under its path relative to the directory as the virtual path, and choosing the smaller of store/deflate per file. validate re-reads every asset and checks its CRC-32, exiting non-zero on any corruption.

Zig library

Add the dependency in build.zig.zon (the package is named open_asset_package; only the CLI binary and the .oap extension use the short form):

.dependencies = .{
    .open_asset_package = .{
        .url = "git+https://gitlab.com/mass4org/mega4/open-asset-package#<rev>",
        .hash = "...",
    },
    // or during local development: .{ .path = "../open-asset-package" },
},

Wire it in build.zig:

const oap_dep = b.dependency("open_asset_package", .{ .target = target, .optimize = optimize });
exe.root_module.addImport("open_asset_package", oap_dep.module("open_asset_package"));

In code a short alias keeps things readable:

const oap = @import("open_asset_package");

Write a package:

const oap = @import("oap");

var w = oap.Writer.init(allocator);
defer w.deinit();
w.setKey(oap.deriveKey("my-secret-passphrase")); // only needed for encryption

try w.add(.{
    .id = my_asset_id,                 // [16]u8
    .vpath = "textures/hero.png",
    .asset_type = 2,                   // your own category byte
    .data = png_bytes,
    .compression = .auto,              // or .{ .fixed = .deflate }
    .encryption = .chacha20,           // or .none (default) / .xor
    .deps = &.{ material_id },
});
try w.setManifest("{\"name\":\"core\",\"version\":\"1.0.0\"}");
try w.writeToFile(io, "core.oap");

Read a package:

var r = try oap.Reader.openFile(io, allocator, "core.oap");
defer r.deinit();
r.setKey(oap.deriveKey("my-secret-passphrase")); // only needed for encryption

const entry = r.findByPath("textures/hero.png") orelse return error.Missing;
const bytes = try r.readAsset(allocator, entry, true); // true = verify CRC
defer allocator.free(bytes);

Reader.initOwned / initCopy open a package already in memory (handy for embedded or network-fetched data, and for true streaming where you fetch the header + index first and range-read individual blobs afterwards).

License

The format specification itself (the contents of SPEC.md) is free for anyone to implement in any project under any license. Format version 1.0.

The source code is GPLv3. Requires Zig 0.16.0. Zero external dependencies.

Part of the Turian game engine ecosystem.

readme_content:
Cambio

A fiat-to-USDC x402 on-ramp, in one Cloudflare Worker — axum on workers-rs (Rust).

A learner generates an EVM keypair in their browser — the private key never leaves the device. They hand Cambio only their public address; Cambio mints a Coinbase Onramp session token and returns a one-click buy URL. They tap it, pay with Apple Pay (real USDC on Base), and spend it as gasless x402 micropayments. The Worker exists for exactly one reason: the Coinbase API secret must never reach a browser.

POST /exchange   {"address":"0x…40 hex…"}
              ->  {"url":"https://pay.coinbase.com/buy?sessionToken=…"}

Non-custodial by construction

Cambio only ever sees a public address. There is no code path that can receive or store a private key. The one secret, CDP_KEY_SECRET, comes only from a Wrangler secret — never logged, never in the repo, never in a response. (CDP_KEY_ID is a public identifier — it appears in every JWT's kid/sub — so it is a plain constant in cambio-onramp, not a secret.)

How it works

  1. Validate the address (0x + 40 hex), rate-limit by address (RL binding).
  2. Mint a CDP EdDSA (Ed25519) JWT — signed with ed25519-dalek (RustCrypto), byte-for-byte identical to the official @coinbase/cdp-sdk output and pinned by cambio-jwt/tests/sdk_conformance.rs (cambio-jwt).
  3. POST https://api.developer.coinbase.com/onramp/v1/token with that JWT.
  4. Return the Coinbase buy URL.

Layout

A three-member Cargo workspace. The two library crates are runtime-agnostic (no workers-rs dependency), so any implementation — CLI, native server, host test — can depend on the signer and money path directly:

  • cambio-jwt/ — the CDP Ed25519 JWT signer. The crown jewel.
  • cambio-onramp/ — the money path: address validation, the Coinbase token request, and buy-URL construction.
  • src/ — the Worker itself: an axum Router (GET/HEAD /, POST /exchange) on workers-rs, the rate-limit binding, and the never-leak error surface.

Supply chain

Pinned and gated. Direct dependencies are exact-=-pinned; the full closure is pinned by the committed Cargo.lock (each checksum line is the integrity gate) and made authoritative by building --locked --offline. Toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml (Rust 1.95.0) and worker-build to 0.8.4. The dependency tree is gated — not merely asserted — by cargo deny (RustSec advisories, a license allow-list, a crates.io-only source policy), run manually before release:

cargo deny check          # advisories + licenses + sources + bans
bash scripts/verify-cargo.sh

See PROVENANCE.md for the pinned versions, the enumerated crypto closure, and the money-path egress audit.

Build & deploy

cargo test -p cambio-jwt -p cambio-onramp                       # SDK conformance + contract tests
cargo build -p cambio --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release # the Worker wasm

npm ci                                # wrangler, from the committed lockfile
wrangler secret put CDP_KEY_SECRET    # the only secret; CDP_KEY_ID is a constant in cambio-onramp
./scripts/deploy.sh                   # bumps the version, runs the conformance gate, worker-build, deploy

License

MIT — see LICENSE. EveryGoodWork's first open-source project.

name: kit-crypto
description: Cryptographic primitives for Kit using Zig std.crypto (no external deps)
readme_content:
kit-crypto

Cryptographic primitives for Kit using Zig std.crypto (no external deps)

[TOC]

Files

File Description
.editorconfig Editor formatting configuration
.gitignore Git ignore rules for build artifacts and dependencies
.tool-versions asdf tool versions (Zig, Kit)
LICENSE MIT license file
README.md This file
docs/.keep Keeps the generated documentation directory present
examples/crypto-hmac.kit HMAC usage example
examples/crypto-kdf.kit Deterministic keyed derivation pattern example
examples/crypto-key-exchange.kit Shared-secret authentication pattern example
examples/crypto-signatures.kit Signature verification pattern example
examples/crypto.kit Basic crypto usage example
kit.toml Package manifest with metadata and dependencies
src/crypto.kit Kit Crypto API
tests/crypto.test.kit Core API tests
tests/function-tests.test.kit Function surface and usage pattern tests
zig/crypto.h C header for the Zig FFI module
zig/crypto.zig Zig implementation using std.crypto
zig/kit_ffi.zig Kit FFI helpers for Zig

Dependencies

No Kit package dependencies.

Installation

kit add gitlab.com/kit-lang/packages/kit-crypto.git

Usage

import Kit.Crypto as Crypto

main = fn =>
  message = "Hello, Kit!"
  secret-key = "my-secret-key"

  # Hash messages with SHA-256 or SHA-512
  sha256-hash = Crypto.sha256 message
  sha512-hash = Crypto.sha512 message

  println "SHA-256: ${sha256-hash}"
  println "SHA-512: ${sha512-hash}"

  # Create HMAC tags for message authentication
  tag = Crypto.hmac-sha256-hex message secret-key
  println "HMAC-SHA256: ${tag}"

  # Verify tags with constant-time comparison
  expected = Crypto.hmac-sha256-hex message secret-key
  is-valid? = Crypto.secure-compare? tag expected
  println "Valid tag: ${is-valid?}"

  # HMAC size helpers return byte counts
  println "HMAC-SHA256 size: ${Crypto.hmac-sha256-size} bytes"
  println "HMAC-SHA512 size: ${Crypto.hmac-sha512-size} bytes"

main

Development

Running Examples

Run examples with the interpreter:

kit run --allow=ffi examples/crypto.kit

Compile examples to a native binary:

kit build examples/crypto.kit --allow=ffi && ./crypto

Running Tests

Run the test suite:

kit test

Run the test suite with coverage:

kit test --coverage

Running kit dev

Run the standard development workflow (build native library, format, check, test):

kit dev

This will:

  1. Build the Zig native library
  2. Format and check source files in src/
  3. Check examples in examples/
  4. Run tests in tests/ with coverage

Running Parity Checks

Check that interpreted examples and compiled examples produce matching output:

kit parity

Generating Documentation

Generate API documentation from doc comments:

kit doc

Note: Kit sources with doc comments (##) will generate HTML documents in docs/*.html

Cleaning Build Artifacts

Remove generated files, caches, and build artifacts:

kit task clean

Note: Defined in kit.toml.

Local Installation

To install this package locally for development:

kit install

This installs the package to ~/.kit/packages/@kit/crypto/, making it available for import as Kit.Crypto in other projects.

License

This package is released under the MIT License - see LICENSE for details.

name: i18n
description: A comprehensive internationalization library for Zig with locale handling, number/date formatting, Unicode normalization, collation, and ICU MessageFormat support
readme_content:
i18n

A comprehensive internationalization library for Zig, backed by ICU4C/CLDR.

Features

  • Locale Handling: Parse and canonicalize BCP47 language tags
  • Number Formatting: Decimal, percent, and currency using ICU number skeletons
  • Date/Time Formatting: Pattern-based formatting with timezone support
  • Calendar Operations: Gregorian and locale-specific calendars
  • Unicode Normalization: NFC, NFD, NFKC, NFKD forms
  • Case Mapping: Locale-aware lowercase/uppercase/titlecase (Turkish-I correct)
  • Collation: Locale-aware string comparison and sort keys
  • Break Iteration: Grapheme, word, line, and sentence segmentation
  • Transliteration: Script conversion (Latin-Greek, Any-Latin, etc.)
  • Translation Catalogs: JSON bundles with ICU MessageFormat (plurals, select, etc.)

Requirements

  • Zig 0.15.1 or later
  • ICU4C 76+ (development packages)

ICU Version Checking

The library requires ICU 76+ by default. You must call checkIcuVersion() at application startup to verify compatibility:

const i18n = @import("i18n");

pub fn main() !void {
    // REQUIRED: Verify ICU version before using any library functions
    try i18n.checkIcuVersion();

    // Now safe to use the library
    // ...
}

If the installed ICU version is below the minimum, checkIcuVersion() returns error.Unsupported. You can customize the minimum version with -Dicu_min_major=N.

Installing ICU

Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt-get install libicu-dev

Fedora:

sudo dnf install libicu-devel

macOS (Homebrew):

brew install icu4c
# May need: -Dicu_prefix=/opt/homebrew/opt/icu4c

Arch Linux:

sudo pacman -S icu

Installation

Using Zig Package Manager

Add to your build.zig.zon:

.dependencies = .{
    .i18n = .{
        .url = "https://gitlab.com/devnw/zig/i18n/-/archive/v0.1.0/i18n-v0.1.0.tar.gz",
        .hash = "...",
    },
},

Then in your build.zig:

const i18n_dep = b.dependency("i18n", .{
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
});
exe.root_module.addImport("i18n", i18n_dep.module("i18n"));

Quick Start

const std = @import("std");
const i18n = @import("i18n");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa = std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator(.{}){};
    defer _ = gpa.deinit();
    const allocator = gpa.allocator();

    // Check ICU version
    try i18n.checkIcuVersion();

    // Format numbers
    const num = try i18n.formatNumberAlloc(allocator, "de-DE", 12345.67);
    defer allocator.free(num);
    std.debug.print("German: {s}\n", .{num}); // "12.345,67"

    // Format currency
    const curr = try i18n.formatCurrencyAlloc(allocator, "en-US", 1234.50, "USD");
    defer allocator.free(curr);
    std.debug.print("USD: {s}\n", .{curr}); // "$1,234.50"

    // Format date/time with timezone
    const dt = try i18n.formatDateTimePatternAlloc(
        allocator,
        "en-US",
        0, // Unix epoch
        "America/New_York",
        "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm zzz",
    );
    defer allocator.free(dt);
    std.debug.print("DateTime: {s}\n", .{dt});

    // Turkish case mapping
    const lower = try i18n.toLowerAlloc(allocator, "tr-TR", "I");
    defer allocator.free(lower);
    std.debug.print("Turkish lowercase I: {s}\n", .{lower}); // "ı" (dotless i)
}

Translation Catalogs

Load JSON translation bundles and format messages with ICU MessageFormat:

const std = @import("std");
const i18n = @import("i18n");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa = std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator(.{}){};
    defer _ = gpa.deinit();
    const allocator = gpa.allocator();

    // Create translation engine
    var engine = try i18n.Engine.init(allocator, "en-US");
    defer engine.deinit();

    // Load JSON bundle
    const json =
        \\{
        \\  "messages": {
        \\    "greeting": "Hello {name}!",
        \\    "items": "{count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}",
        \\    "total": "Total: {amount, number, ::currency/USD}"
        \\  }
        \\}
    ;
    try engine.addJsonBundle("en-US", json);

    // Format messages with named arguments
    const greeting = try engine.tAlloc(allocator, "en-US", "messages.greeting", .{
        .name = "World",
    });
    defer allocator.free(greeting);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{greeting}); // "Hello World!"

    // Plural handling
    const items = try engine.tAlloc(allocator, "en-US", "messages.items", .{
        .count = 5,
    });
    defer allocator.free(items);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{items}); // "5 items"

    // Currency in message
    const total = try engine.tAlloc(allocator, "en-US", "messages.total", .{
        .amount = 99.99,
    });
    defer allocator.free(total);
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{total}); // "Total: $99.99"
}

Build Options

Option Description Default
-Dicu_prefix=/path Custom ICU installation path (skips pkg-config) (none)
-Dicu_min_major=N Minimum required ICU major version 76
-Dstrings_path=/path Optional strings module to import (none)
-Dtransliteration_max_input=N Max UTF-8 input bytes for transliteration 1048576
-Dicu_enabled=false Build without ICU dependencies (features return Error.Unsupported) true

Example with custom ICU:

zig build -Dicu_prefix=/opt/icu76

API Overview

Numbers

  • formatNumberAlloc(allocator, locale, value) - Format decimal number
  • formatNumberSkeletonAlloc(allocator, locale, value, skeleton) - Format with ICU skeleton
  • formatCurrencyAlloc(allocator, locale, value, currency_code) - Format currency

Date/Time

  • formatDateTimePatternAlloc(allocator, locale, instant_ms, tzid, pattern) - Format date/time

Calendar

  • Calendar.init(allocator, locale, tzid) - Create calendar
  • cal.set(year, month, day, hour, minute, second) - Set date/time
  • cal.toInstantMs() - Get Unix milliseconds

Unicode

  • normalizeAlloc(allocator, form, input) - Normalize (NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD)
  • toLowerAlloc(allocator, locale, input) - Locale-aware lowercase
  • toUpperAlloc(allocator, locale, input) - Locale-aware uppercase
  • toTitleAlloc(allocator, locale, input) - Locale-aware title case

Collation

  • compare(allocator, locale, a, b) - Compare strings (.lt, .eq, .gt)
  • Collator.init(allocator, locale) - Create reusable collator

Break Iteration

  • graphemeCount(allocator, locale, text) - Count grapheme clusters
  • BreakIterator.init(allocator, type, locale) - Create break iterator

Transliteration

  • transliterateAlloc(allocator, id, input) - Transliterate text

Raw ICU Access

  • i18n.icu - Direct access to ICU C bindings for advanced use

Thread Safety

The library is designed for concurrent use with the following model:

Stateless Functions (Thread-Safe)

All formatting functions are stateless and safe to call from multiple threads:

  • formatNumberAlloc, formatCurrencyAlloc, formatDateTimePatternAlloc
  • normalizeAlloc, toLowerAlloc, toUpperAlloc, toTitleAlloc
  • compare, transliterateAlloc, graphemeCount

Translation Engine (Two-Phase Model)

The Engine type requires careful handling:

// PHASE 1: Initialization (single-threaded)
var engine = try i18n.Engine.init(allocator, "en-US");
try engine.addJsonBundle("en-US", en_json);
try engine.addJsonBundle("de-DE", de_json);

// PHASE 2: Usage (multi-threaded safe)
// After all bundles are loaded, tAlloc() is safe to call concurrently
// Do NOT call addJsonBundle() during this phase
const msg = try engine.tAlloc(allocator, "en-US", "key", .{});

Security Considerations

JSON Bundle Size Limits

The Engine.addJsonBundle() function parses JSON input without an inherent size limit. If your application accepts translation bundles from untrusted sources, validate the input size before calling this function to prevent memory exhaustion attacks:

const MAX_BUNDLE_SIZE = 10 * 1024 * 1024; // 10 MB
if (json_bytes.len > MAX_BUNDLE_SIZE) {
    return error.BundleTooLarge;
}
try engine.addJsonBundle(locale, json_bytes);

JSON Bundle Depth Limits

Translation bundles are flattened recursively. To avoid stack exhaustion with deeply nested JSON, the engine enforces a maximum depth (catalog.MAX_BUNDLE_DEPTH). Inputs that exceed this return Error.JsonTooDeep.

Transliteration Input Limits

Transliteration enforces a maximum input size (transliteration.MAX_TRANSLITERATION_INPUT_BYTES) to prevent excessive memory usage. You can override this via -Dtransliteration_max_input=N if your application needs higher limits.

ICU Optional Mode

If ICU is not available in your environment, build with -Dicu_enabled=false. ICU-dependent APIs will return Error.Unsupported instead of panicking or crashing, while JSON bundle management still works for simple lookup without formatting arguments.

Input Validation

  • UTF-8: All string inputs are validated by ICU. Invalid UTF-8 sequences return Error.InvalidUtf8.
  • Locale tags: Invalid or malformed locale tags return Error.InvalidLocale.
  • Calendar values: Month (1-12), day (1-31), and time components are validated.
  • Currency codes: Must be exactly 3 ASCII letters (e.g., "USD").

Running Tests

# Run all tests
zig build test

# Run tests directly
zig test src/i18n_test.zig

# Run integration tests
zig build test-integration

License

  • This library: Apache License 2.0
  • ICU4C: Unicode License (https://www.unicode.org/copyright.html)

See the LICENSE file for details.

Contributing

See CONTRIBUTING.md for guidelines.

Security

See SECURITY.md for security policy and vulnerability reporting.

name: hsm
description: Zig Hardware Security Module library for PIV, CAC, and YubiKey tokens via PC/SC. Supports certificates, PIN management, signing, and decryption.
readme_content:
zhsm

A Hardware Security Module (HSM) library for Zig providing PC/SC access to PIV, CAC, and YubiKey tokens.

Status

Aspect Info
API Stability Development
Zig Version 0.16.0
Platforms Linux, macOS, Windows
License MIT

Features

  • PIV Support (NIST SP 800-73-4)

    • Certificate retrieval (slots 9A, 9C, 9D, 9E)
    • PIN verification, change, and unblock
    • ECDSA P-256/P-384 signing
    • RSA 2048/3072/4096 signing
    • RSA decryption

  • CAC Support (Common Access Card)

    • Modern PIV-compatible CACs (full operations)
    • Legacy CAC PKI applet detection (applet selection only)

  • YubiKey Support

    • PIV applet operations
    • ATR-based detection
    • Optional management commands

  • Security

    • No secrets in logs (redacted debug mode)
    • Sensitive buffer zeroization
    • Strict TLV parsing with depth/length limits
    • Tight error types (no anyerror)
    • Session-bound PIN verification (ATR-based card swap detection)

  • Parallel Operations (via thread_pool)

    • Batch signing across multiple slots
    • Batch decryption across multiple keys
    • Parallel token discovery across readers
    • Parallel certificate retrieval across slots
    • Automatic sequential fallback below threshold (< 2 items)
    • Enabled by default (-Denable_tp=true); disable with -Denable_tp=false

Requirements

  • Zig 0.16.0 or compatible
  • PC/SC Library:
    • Linux: libpcsclite-dev (Debian/Ubuntu) or pcsc-lite-devel (Fedora)
    • macOS: Built-in PCSC.framework
    • Windows: Built-in Winscard.dll

Installing PC/SC on Linux

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install libpcsclite-dev pcscd

# Fedora/RHEL
sudo dnf install pcsc-lite-devel pcsc-lite

# Start the PC/SC daemon
sudo systemctl start pcscd
sudo systemctl enable pcscd

Building

# Build and run unit tests
make

# Or using zig directly
zig build test

# Run simulator integration tests
zig build test -Dintegration_sim=true

# Build examples (requires PC/SC library installed)
zig build examples -Dlink_pcsc=true

Build Options

Option Default Description Security Impact
integration_sim false Run simulator integration tests None
hsm_hil false Run hardware-in-loop tests (requires real token) None
link_pcsc false Link PC/SC library for examples None
include_simulator Debug: true
Release: false		 Include PIV simulator with test keys CWE-321: Test keys in production
allow_pcsc_env_override false SECURITY RISK: Allow HSM_PCSC_LIB_PATH env var CWE-427: Untrusted library loading
fips false Route security crypto through the linked FIPS-140-3 provider (zero overhead when off) None when off
openssl_path (unset) OpenSSL install prefix for non-standard installs (e.g. /usr/local/ssl) None

FIPS-140-3 / PQC mode

With -Dfips=true, every security-relevant cryptographic primitive routes through a linked, validated OpenSSL 3.x FIPS provider via the crypto_backend seam, and the simulator gains post-quantum PIV token operations (ML-DSA-65 signing, ML-KEM-768 encap/decap) that are available only in FIPS mode. The flag is off by default with zero overhead; the fips dependency is resolved only under -Dfips=true.

# Default build — std.crypto backend, no OpenSSL link
zig build test

# FIPS build — OpenSSL FIPS provider (run `make deps` from fips first)
OPENSSL_CONF=/usr/local/ssl/ssl/openssl.cnf \
  zig build test -Dfips=true -Dopenssl_path=/usr/local/ssl

# Both modes in one shot
make test-dual

See docs/FIPS.md for the seam design, the fips-exempt policy, and the PQC token operations.

Security Note: The allow_pcsc_env_override option is disabled by default to prevent malicious library injection attacks (CWE-427). Only enable this for development/testing:

# Production build (secure, env var ignored)
zig build

# Development build (allows HSM_PCSC_LIB_PATH)
zig build -Dallow_pcsc_env_override=true

When enabled, libraries are validated before loading:

  • Must be absolute paths
  • Cannot be world-writable
  • Warns on group-writable files

Quick Start

const std = @import("std");
const hsm = @import("hsm");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa = std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator(.{}){};
    defer _ = gpa.deinit();
    const allocator = gpa.allocator();

    // List available tokens
    const tokens = try hsm.listTokens(allocator, false);
    defer {
        for (tokens) |*t| t.deinit();
        allocator.free(tokens);
    }

    if (tokens.len == 0) {
        std.debug.print("No tokens found\n", .{});
        return;
    }

    // Open the first token
    var token = try hsm.openToken(allocator, tokens[0].id, .{});
    defer token.close();

    // Verify PIN
    try token.verifyPin("123456");

    // Read certificate
    const cert = try token.getCertificate(.authentication);
    defer allocator.free(cert);
    std.debug.print("Certificate: {} bytes\n", .{cert.len});

    // Sign a digest
    var digest: [32]u8 = undefined;
    std.crypto.hash.sha2.Sha256.hash("Hello, PIV!", &digest, .{});

    const signature = try token.sign(.authentication, .ecdsa_p256, &digest);
    defer allocator.free(signature);
    std.debug.print("Signature: {} bytes\n", .{signature.len});
}

API Overview

Types

Type Description
TokenKind Token type: .piv, .cac, .yubikey, .unknown
TokenInfo Discovered token metadata
Token Open token handle for operations
Slot Key slot: .authentication (9A), .signature (9C), .key_management (9D), .card_auth (9E)
Algorithm Crypto algorithm: .ecdsa_p256, .ecdsa_p384, .rsa2048_pkcs1v15, etc.
Capabilities Token capability flags
PcscScope PC/SC context scope: .user (default), .system

Functions

Function Description
listTokens(allocator, use_sim) List available tokens
openToken(allocator, id, opts) Open a token by ID
token.reconnect() Reconnect to token and reset auth state
token.verifyPin(pin) Verify PIN
token.changePin(old, new) Change PIN
token.unblockPin(puk, new_pin) Unblock PIN with PUK
token.getCertificate(slot) Get DER-encoded certificate
token.sign(slot, alg, digest) Sign a digest
token.decrypt(slot, alg, ciphertext) Decrypt data
token.capabilities() Get token capabilities
token.close() Close token connection

Errors

All operations return errors from HsmError:

  • PC/SC: PcscUnavailable, ReaderGone, CardRemoved, Timeout
  • PIN: PinIncorrect, PinLocked, PinLengthInvalid
  • Capability: NotSupported, SlotNotFound, AlgorithmNotSupported
  • Data: InvalidTlv, CertificateNotFound, InvalidDigestLength
  • Security: SecurityConditionNotSatisfied, AuthenticationFailed

Parallel Operations Module

The parallel module provides batch HSM operations using the thread_pool library. It is built as a separate Zig module and available when -Denable_tp=true (the default). Set -Denable_tp=false to compile out the seam entirely; the public functions still exist and fall back to a sequential implementation.

Function Description Threshold
parallelSign(allocator, inputs, results) Batch signing across slots 2+ items
parallelDecrypt(allocator, inputs, results) Batch decryption across keys 2+ items
parallelTokenDiscover(readers, results) Token discovery across readers 2+ readers
parallelCertRetrieve(allocator, requests, results) Certificate retrieval across slots 2+ requests

Below the threshold, operations execute sequentially without thread pool overhead. The underlying PKCS#11 calls are scaffolding; integrate your PKCS#11 backend by implementing the signData, decryptData, discoverToken, and retrieveCert functions in src/parallel.zig.

Testing

Unit Tests

# Run all unit tests
zig build test

Simulator Integration Tests

The library includes a PIV card simulator for testing without hardware:

# Run simulator tests
zig build test -Dintegration_sim=true

The simulator uses embedded test keys (see src/sim/key_material.zig). No external key files or environment variables are needed.

Hardware-in-Loop (HIL) Tests

For testing with real hardware:

# Read-only tests (certificate reading)
HSM_HIL=1 zig build test -Dhsm_hil=true

# Tests requiring PIN
HSM_HIL=1 HSM_PIN=123456 zig build test -Dhsm_hil=true

# Dangerous tests (write operations) - USE WITH CAUTION
HSM_HIL=1 HSM_PIN=123456 HSM_DANGEROUS=1 zig build test -Dhsm_hil=true

Fuzz Testing

# Continuous fuzzing (stop manually)
zig build test --fuzz -- --test-filter fuzz

Examples

# Build examples (requires PC/SC library installed)
zig build examples -Dlink_pcsc=true

# List tokens
./zig-out/bin/list_tokens
./zig-out/bin/list_tokens --sim  # Use simulator

# Sign with PIV (PIN entered via interactive TTY prompt)
./zig-out/bin/piv_sign
./zig-out/bin/piv_sign --sim

# Or supply PIN via environment variable (less secure)
HSM_PIN=123456 ./zig-out/bin/piv_sign --sim

Security Notes

  1. PIN Handling: PINs are never stored in token structures and are zeroized after use.

  2. TLV Parsing: All TLV parsing has depth (10) and length (64KB) limits to prevent resource exhaustion.

  3. Error Handling: Unknown status words result in explicit errors, not silent failures.

  4. Logging: Debug logging never includes sensitive data (PINs, keys, etc.).

  5. Memory: Sensitive buffers are zeroized using hsm.zeroize() which prevents compiler optimization.

  6. PC/SC Library Loading: The library loads PC/SC from trusted absolute paths. An explicit override is available via HSM_PCSC_LIB_PATH (must be absolute).

Observability

hsm ships an opt-in OpenTelemetry seam for span tracing of HSM operations. The seam is off by default and produces zero overhead when off — the build never resolves the otel dependency, every helper compiles to a comptime-known no-op, and the produced artifacts contain no otel or observability linked symbols.

Enabling

zig build test                  # default: -Dwith_otel=false (no-op)
zig build test -Dwith_otel=true # opt in: spans emitted

When enabled, every public Token.sign / Token.decrypt call emits an hsm.{operation} span (e.g. hsm.sign, hsm.decrypt) with two attributes:

  • crypto.algorithm — algorithm tag (e.g. ecdsa_p256, rsa2048_pkcs1v15).
  • crypto.key.id — slot identifier (e.g. authentication, signature, key_management, card_auth).

Security contract

The seam is engineered around one rule: NEVER export cryptographic material. Span attributes are exported off-host (typically to an OTLP collector) and end up in traces/logs that may have weaker access controls than the HSM operation itself.

  • Private key bytes, plaintext, ciphertext, signatures, digests, and PINs are NEVER attached to spans by this library.
  • Only operation type, slot identifier, and algorithm name leave the process via telemetry.
  • If your application's slot identifiers are themselves sensitive (e.g. correlated with user identity), redact or hash them before passing to hsm.observability.startHsmOperationSpan.

Process bootstrap

const hsm = @import("hsm");

pub fn main() !void {
    // Park the Otel value on a stable address — either a `var` in
    // main()'s stack frame for the process lifetime, or a heap
    // allocation. The init helper is only present when
    // `-Dwith_otel=true`; under the disabled build,
    // hsm.observability_init resolves to an empty struct and this
    // block compiles to a no-op.
    if (comptime hsm.observability.enabled) {
        var otel = try hsm.observability_init.Otel.init(allocator, "my-service");
        defer otel.deinit();
        otel.installGlobals();
    }
    // ... rest of main, including any hsm.Token.sign calls — each one
    // now emits an `hsm.sign` span attached to your service.
}

The seam reads OTEL_* environment variables (sampler, exporter endpoint, service.name, etc.) per the OpenTelemetry environment-variable spec. Defaults: parentbased_traceidratio sampler at 5%, OTLP/HTTP-protobuf exporter to http://localhost:4318.

Recipe + verification

The full integration recipe (build wiring, test harness, no-op verifier) is documented in the otel rollout repo: otel/docs/integration/RECIPE.md.

Three gates must pass before merging changes that touch the seam:

zig build test                                 # default flag = false
zig build test -Dwith_otel=true                # flag on
scripts/verify-consumer-noop.sh                # symbol-leak check

The verify-consumer-noop.sh gate builds the library with -Dwith_otel=false and walks zig-out/ with nm --defined-only, failing if any otel/observability symbol survived into the artifacts. It mirrors the cross-repo otel/scripts/verify-consumer- noop.sh (which only runs in the sibling-repo layout <root>/otel//<root>/hsm/) so contributors without that layout can still gate the seam locally.

Project Structure

src/
├── hsm.zig              # Main API and types
├── root.zig             # Module entry point
├── apdu.zig             # APDU encoding/decoding
├── tlv.zig              # BER-TLV parsing
├── parallel.zig         # Parallel operations (thread_pool)
├── pcsc/
│   └── pcsc.zig         # PC/SC transport layer (Linux/macOS/Windows)
├── piv/
│   └── piv.zig          # PIV implementation
├── cac/
│   └── cac.zig          # CAC implementation
├── yubikey/
│   └── yubikey.zig      # YubiKey detection
└── sim/
    ├── sim.zig          # Simulator entry point
    ├── transport.zig    # Simulated transport
    ├── piv_card.zig     # Simulated PIV card
    └── key_material.zig # Embedded test keys

tests/
├── integration.zig      # Basic integration tests
├── sim_integration.zig  # Simulator integration tests
└── hil_tests.zig        # Hardware-in-loop tests

examples/
├── list_tokens.zig      # Token discovery example
└── piv_sign.zig         # Signing example

References

  • NIST SP 800-73-4 - PIV Specification
  • FIPS 201-3 - PIV Standard
  • PC/SC Workgroup - PC/SC Specifications
  • Yubico PIV Tool - YubiKey PIV Documentation

Contributing

See CONTRIBUTING.md for guidelines.

name: stdx
description: extensions for the zig standard library
readme_content:
Overview

This is a library adding several generally useful tools that are either not included in the standard library or have slightly different behavior. As the zig programming language matures, we should get more and more awesome std library features but until then...

All data structures, algorithms and utilities included in this library are written from scratch. This minimizes the threat of malicious or unintentional supply chain attacks. It also ensures that all code is controlled in a single place and HOPEFULLY minimizes the chance that zig turns into the hellish monstrocity that is npm and the nodejs ecosystem.

In general people use this library for the RingBuffer and the MemoryPool datastructures. See below for details.

Mirrors and Sources:

  • GitLab source repo
  • Github mirror

Table of Contents

  1. Overview
    1. Usage
    2. Installation
    3. Organization
    4. Examples
    5. Benchmarks
    6. Contributing
    7. Code of Conduct
  2. Documentation
    1. stdx
      1. BufferedChannel
      2. UnbufferedChannel
      3. Signal
      4. EventEmitter
      5. ManagedQueue
      6. UnmanagedQueue
      7. RingBuffer
      8. SPSCQueue
      9. MemoryPool

Usage

zig version stdx version
0.15.x 0.2.1
0.16.0 0.3.0+

Using stdx is just as simple as using any other zig dependency.

// import the library into your file
const stdx = @import("stdx");

fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    // your code
    // ....

    const memory_pool = try stdx.MemoryPool(i32).init(allocator, io, 200);
    defer memory_pool.deinit();

    // your code
    // ...
}

Installation

Install using zig fetch

zig fetch --save  https://gitlab.com/kobolds-io/stdx/-/archive/v0.4.2/stdx-v0.4.2.tar.gz

Alternatively, you can install stdx just like any other zig dependency by editing your build.zig.zon file.

    .dependencies = .{
        .stdx = .{
            .url = "https://gitlab.com/kobolds-io/stdx/-/archive/v0.4.2/stdx-v0.4.2.tar.gz",
            .hash = "<hash>",
        },
    },

run zig build --fetch to fetch the dependencies. This will return an error as the has will not match. Copy the new hash and try again.Sometimes zig is helpful and it caches stuff for you in the zig-cache dir. Try deleting that directory if you see some issues.

In the build.zig file add the library as a dependency.

// ...boilerplate

const stdx_dep = b.dependency("stdx", .{
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
});
const stdx_mod = stdx_dep.module("stdx");

exe.root_module.addImport("stdx", stdx_mod);

Organization

This library organized as stdx.<DataStructure/Algorithm>. Very simple.

Examples

There are examples included in this library that go over a brief overview of how each feature can be used. You can build and run examples by performing the following steps. Examples are in the examples directory. Examples are always welcome.


# add optimization flags if you want ;)
zig build examples

./zig-out/bin/<example_name>

Examples are best used if you modify the code and add print statements to figure out what is going on. Look at the source code files for additional tips on how features work by taking a look at the tests included in the source code.

Benchmarks

There are benchmarks included in this library that you can run your local hardware or target hardware. You can run benchmarksby performing the following steps. Benchmarks are in the benchmarks directory. More benchmarks are always welcome. Benchmarks in this library are written using zbench by hendriknielander. Please check out that repo and star it and support other zig developers.

Note Benchmarks are always a point of contention between everyone. One of my goals is to provision some hardware in the cloud that is consistently used as the hardware for all comparisons. Until then, you can run the code locally to test out your performance. These benchmarks are run inside of a virtual machine and the CPU is fully emulated. This means you will see better performance on your native machines.

# with standard optimizations (debug build)
zig build bench

# or with more optimizations
zig build bench -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe

Contributing

Please see Contributing for more information on how to get involved.

Code of Conduct

Please see the Code of Conduct file. Simple library, simple rules.

Documentation

stdx

The stdx top level module and should be imported as const stdx = @import("stdx"); or importing structures directly using const RingBuffer = @import("stdx").RingBuffer;.

BufferedChannel

added v0.0.3 as stdx.BufferedChannel

The BufferedChannel is a structure that can be used to safely transmit data across threads. It uses a backing buffer which stores the actual values transmitted. Additionally it has a very simple api send/receive and supports concepts like cancellation and timeouts.

See example and source for more information on usage.

UnbufferedChannel

added v0.0.3 as stdx.UnbufferedChannel

The UnbufferedChannel is a structure that can be used to safely transmit data across threads. It uses a Condition to notify receivers that there is new data. Additionally it has a very simple api send/receive and supports concepts like timeouts but does not currently support cancellation.

See example and source for more information on usage.

Signal

added v0.0.8 as stdx.Signal

The Signal is a structure that can be used to safely transmit data across threads. Unlike a channel, it does not require that both threads become synchronized at the same point. Think of a Signal as a way for a sender to throw a value over the fence and a receiver to pick the value at a later time (when it is convenient for the receiver). Signals are "one shots", meaning that they should only ever be used once. These structures are ideal for things like request->reply kinds of problems.

See example and source for more information on usage.

ManagedQueue

added v0.0.2 as stdx.ManagedQueue

The ManagedQueue is a generic queue implementation that uses a singly linked list. It allows for the management of a queue with operations like enqueueing, dequeueing, checking if the queue is empty, concatenating two queues, and handles the allocation/deallocation of memory used by the queue. The queue is managed by an allocator, which is used for creating and destroying nodes.

See example and source for more information on usage.

UnmanagedQueue

added v0.0.2 as stdx.UnmanagedQueue

The UnmanagedQueue is a generic queue implementation that uses a singly linked list. It most closely represents the std.SinglyLinkedList in its functionality. Differing from the ManagedQueue, the UnmanagedQueue requires memory allocations to be external to the queue and provides a generic Node structure to help link everything together.

Please also see UnmanagedQueueNode which is the Node used by the UnmanagedQueue.

See example and source for more information on usage.

RingBuffer

added v0.0.1 as stdx.RingBuffer

A RingBuffer is a data structure that is really useful for managing memory in a fixed memory allocation. This particular implementation is particularly useful for a fixed size queue. Kobolds uses the RingBuffer data structure for inboxes and outboxes for when messages are received/sent through TCP connections.

See example and source for more information on usage.

SPSCQueue

added v0.4.0 as stdx.SPSCQueue

SPSCQueue is a lock-free, atomic queue for passing data safely between one producer thread and one consumer thread. It behaves like a lightweight channel, but avoids locks and blocking, making it a good fit for high-throughput, one-way handoff between threads. Use it when data only needs to flow in one direction and you want predictable, low-overhead communication.

See example and source for more information on usage.

MemoryPool

added v0.0.1 as stdx.MemoryPool

A MemoryPool is a structure that uses pre-allocated blocks of memory to quickly allocoate and deallocate resources quickly. It is very useful in situations where you have statically allocated memory but you will have fluctuating usage of that memory. A good example would be handling messages flowing throughout a system.

See example and source for more information on usage.

EventEmitter

added v0.0.6 as stdx.EventEmitter

The EventEmitter is a tool for managing communications across callbacks. This is a very similar implementation to the nodejs event emitter class which is one of the fundemental building blocks for asynchronous events. The EventEmitter provides a simple(ish) api to register Callbacks with appropriate Contexts to be called when a specific Event is called.

See example and source for more information on usage.

name: gnoll
description: zig application configuration handled well
readme_content:
Gnoll

gnoll is a simple library that helps you load your configs from files. It currently supports the following file formats.

  • json
  • yaml

gnoll is no real substitute for a well thoughtout configuration system but will play nicely with application code.

Note: code/issues and all work are hosted at https://gitlab.com/kobolds-io/gnoll

Usage

Using gnoll is pretty simple.

// import the library into your file
const gnoll = @import("gnoll");
const Gnoll = gnoll.Gnoll;
const ConfigInfo = gnoll.ConfigInfo; // if you like types
const GnollOptions = gnoll.GnollOptions; // if you like types

// Define your config type
const TestConfig = struct {
    key_0: u32,
    key_1: []const u8,
    key_2: struct {
        key_0: []f32,
    },
};

fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    // Define some filepaths to check for configuration files
    const gnoll_options = GnollOptions{
        .config_infos = &.{
            // if we can't find this file, fallback to the next one etc...
            ConfigInfo{
                .filepath = "./test_data/config_0.json",
                .format = .json,
            },
            ConfigInfo{
                .filepath = "./test_data/config_1.yaml",
                .format = .yaml,
            },
        },
    };

    // Initialize Gnoll with your config Type
    var gnoll = try Gnoll(TestConfig).init(allocator, io, gnoll_options);
    defer gnoll.deinit(allocator);

    // get values from `gnoll` after initialization
    std.debug.print("key_0 value: {d}\n", .{gnoll.config.key_0});
    std.debug.print("key_2.key_0 value: {any}\n", .{gnoll.config.key_2.key_0});
}

Installation

zig version stdx version
0.15.x 0.1.0
0.16.0 0.2.x

You can install gnoll just like any other zig dependency by editing your build.zig.zon file or by using the zig fetch command.

zig fetch --save https://gitlab.com/kobolds-io/gnoll/-/archive/v0.2.1/gnoll-v0.2.1.tar.gz

In your build.zig file add the library as a dependency.

// ...boilerplate

const gnoll_dep = b.dependency("gnoll", .{
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
});
const gnoll_mod = gnoll_dep.module("gnoll");

exe.root_module.addImport("gnoll", gnoll_mod);

Overview

gnoll works by cycling through the passed GnollOptions during the init function call to find a valid configuration. Once a configuration file exists on the file system, gnoll will use the appropriate parser to load into the gnoll.config field. Overall, pretty simple but nice and useful.

Features

Feature Implemented
json support yes
yaml support yes
toml support no
do not immediately fail on first failed parsed no

name: mcp
description: A Zig implementation of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) spec revision 2025-03-26. Features JSON-RPC 2.0, stdio/HTTP transports, OAuth2.1 authentication, worker thread pool with cancellation, and deterministic testing.
readme_content:
mcp - MCP Server Library for Zig

A Zig 0.15.2 implementation of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) spec revision 2025-03-26.

Status

Aspect Info
API Stability Beta
Zig Version 0.15.2+
Platforms Linux, macOS, Windows

Features

  • JSON-RPC 2.0 - Single and batch message support, string/integer IDs
  • Transports - stdio (newline-delimited) and Streamable HTTP with SSE
  • Authentication - Bearer, Basic, and OAuth2.1 with embedded endpoints
  • Parallel Handling - Worker thread pool with cancellation support
  • Deterministic Testing - Barrier tool for proving parallelism without timing

Protocol Version

2025-03-26

Requirements

  • Zig 0.15.2+
  • Local ../json dependency (RFC 8259 JSON parser)

Installation

Add to your build.zig.zon:

.dependencies = .{
    .mcp = .{
        .path = "../mcp", // or URL to tarball
    },
},

In build.zig:

const mcp_dep = b.dependency("mcp", .{ .target = target, .optimize = optimize });
exe.root_module.addImport("mcp", mcp_dep.module("mcp"));

Quick Start

const std = @import("std");
const mcp = @import("mcp");

pub fn main() !void {
    var gpa = std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator(.{}){};
    defer _ = gpa.deinit();
    const allocator = gpa.allocator();

    var server = try mcp.Server.init(allocator, .{
        .name = "my-server",
        .version = "1.0.0",
        .worker_threads = 4,
    }, MyHandler.create());
    defer server.deinit();

    // stdio transport
    try server.serveStdio();

    // or HTTP transport
    // const port = try server.serveHttp();
}

Public API

pub const ProtocolVersion = "2025-03-26";

pub const AuthMode = enum { none, bearer, basic, oauth2 };

pub const ServerOptions = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    version: []const u8,
    instructions: ?[]const u8 = null,
    worker_threads: u16 = 0,
    max_message_bytes: usize = 8 * 1024 * 1024,
    max_batch_items: u32 = 256,
    max_inflight: u32 = 1024,
    http_bind: []const u8 = "127.0.0.1",
    http_port: u16 = 0,
    http_path: []const u8 = "/mcp",
    http_allow_origin: ?[]const u8 = null,
    auth_mode: AuthMode = .none,
    bearer_token: ?[]const u8 = null,
    basic_user: ?[]const u8 = null,
    basic_pass: ?[]const u8 = null,
};

pub const CancelToken = struct {
    pub fn isCancelled(self: *const CancelToken) bool;
};

pub const Session = struct {
    pub fn notify(self: *Session, method: []const u8, params_json: ?[]const u8) anyerror!void;
    pub fn request(self: *Session, method: []const u8, params_json: ?[]const u8, timeout_ms: u32) anyerror![]const u8;
};

pub const Handler = struct {
    ctx: ?*anyopaque = null,
    listTools: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, cursor: ?[]const u8) anyerror![]const u8,
    callTool: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, name: []const u8, args_json: []const u8, cancel: *const CancelToken) anyerror![]const u8,
    listResources: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, cursor: ?[]const u8) anyerror![]const u8,
    readResource: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, uri: []const u8) anyerror![]const u8,
    listResourceTemplates: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque) anyerror![]const u8,
    subscribeResource: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, uri: []const u8) anyerror!void,
    listPrompts: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, cursor: ?[]const u8) anyerror![]const u8,
    getPrompt: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, name: []const u8, args_json: ?[]const u8) anyerror![]const u8,
    complete: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, params_json: []const u8) anyerror![]const u8,
    setLogLevel: *const fn(ctx: ?*anyopaque, level: []const u8) anyerror!void,
};

pub const Server = struct {
    pub fn init(a: std.mem.Allocator, opt: ServerOptions, h: Handler) anyerror!Server;
    pub fn deinit(self: *Server) void;
    pub fn serveStdio(self: *Server) anyerror!void;
    pub fn serveHttp(self: *Server) anyerror!u16;
    pub fn stop(self: *Server) void;
};

Testing

# Run all tests
zig build test

# Run acceptance tests only
zig build test-accept

Acceptance Tests

Test Description
T1 stdio init+initialized+ping => correct responses
T2 stdio batch of 2 pings => ordered batch response
T3 stdio batch of 2 barrier calls => proves parallelism
T4 HTTP bearer: 401 without auth, 200 with token + session ID
T5 HTTP oauth2: well-known endpoint returns metadata

MCP Methods Supported

Lifecycle

  • initialize / notifications/initialized
  • ping
  • notifications/cancelled
  • notifications/progress

Tools

  • tools/list (with cursor pagination)
  • tools/call

Resources

  • resources/list
  • resources/read

Tasks

  • tasks/get
  • tasks/list (cursor + limit pagination; returns nextCursor when more results are available)
  • tasks/cancel
  • tasks/result
  • resources/templates/list
  • resources/subscribe

Prompts

  • prompts/list
  • prompts/get

Logging

  • logging/setLevel
  • notifications/message

Completion

  • completion/complete (ref/prompt + ref/resource, ≤100 results)

Authentication

Bearer Token

.auth_mode = .bearer,
.bearer_token = "my-secret-token",

Basic Auth

.auth_mode = .basic,
.basic_user = "admin",
.basic_pass = "password",

OAuth2.1

.auth_mode = .oauth2,

Provides endpoints:

  • /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
  • /mcp/authorize
  • /mcp/token
  • /mcp/register

Observability

Optional OpenTelemetry instrumentation for MCP request/response paths. Off by default — when -Dwith_otel=false (the default), the otel dependency is never fetched and the produced artifacts contain zero otel/observability symbols (verified by verify-consumer-noop.sh from the otel toolchain).

Build flag

zig build -Dwith_otel=true                # compile with otel
zig build test -Dwith_otel=true           # run smoke test
zig build                                 # default = disabled, zero overhead

Spans emitted

Both client (outgoing) and server (incoming) JSON-RPC paths produce spans with otel rpc.* semantic conventions:

  • rpc.system = "mcp"
  • rpc.method = "<json-rpc method>" (e.g. "tools/call", "resources/list")
  • span kind: .client for outbound Session.request, .server for inbound Server.processJsonValue
  • on JSON-RPC errors, rpc.jsonrpc.error_code is attached and span status is set to error

Bootstrap

const std = @import("std");
const mcp = @import("mcp");

pub fn main() !void {
    var otel = try mcp.observability_init.Otel.init(allocator, "my-service");
    defer otel.deinit();
    otel.installGlobals();
    // ... your MCP server / client ...
}

OTEL_* env vars (e.g. OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER) are honoured by the bootstrap helper. Telemetry is non-fatal: a failing exporter never breaks MCP traffic.

For full integration details see the otel rollout recipe at devnw/zig/otel/docs/integration/RECIPE.md.

License

Apache-2.0 License - see LICENSE for details.

Rationale

  • Single-file design minimizes module complexity for MCP server use case
  • Handler callbacks return JSON strings for zero-copy response embedding
  • Barrier tool uses atomics for deterministic parallelism proof without timing
  • OAuth2.1 metadata endpoint enables client autodiscovery
  • SSE connections tracked per session for server→client messaging
  • Thread pool workers check shutdown flag at 1ms intervals for responsive stop
  • Batch processing preserves response order via sequential ArrayList append

name: ds
description: High-performance data structures and algorithms library for Zig. Includes graphs, trees, caching, string search, and serialization (DOT/GQL).
readme_content:
SPYDER Data Structures - Zig Implementation

High-performance, deterministic data structures and graph analytics library for Zig 0.16.0.

This is a complete Zig port of the Go implementation at go.spyder.org/ds, providing full parity with all features, tests, and benchmarks.

Status

🎉 ALL PHASES COMPLETE - Production Ready ✅

Completed Components

Phase 1: Foundation & Build System

  • ✅ Build system (build.zig, build.zig.zon)
  • ✅ Stack (generic LIFO)
  • ✅ Queue (FIFO queue backed by a ring buffer)
  • ✅ Deque (double-ended queue with ring buffer)
  • ✅ Set/MultiSet (hash-based)
  • ✅ Tests for all Phase 1 components
  • ✅ Benchmark infrastructure

Phase 2: Tree Structures

  • ✅ BST (Binary Search Tree - unbalanced)
  • ✅ RBTree (Red-Black Tree with insert/delete)
  • ✅ SkipList (probabilistic balancing with seeded PRNG)
  • ✅ Trie (prefix tree with Unicode support)
  • ✅ Tests for all tree structures
  • ⏳ B+Tree (deferred to later phase)

Phase 3: Graph Core

  • ✅ Vertex (generic node with ID, value, edges)
  • ✅ Edge (tagged union: basic, directed, weighted, directed+weighted)
  • ✅ Graph (thread-safe add/remove operations)
  • ✅ Version tracking for mutation detection
  • ✅ Helper methods (findVertexById, getLeaves)
  • ✅ Comprehensive tests for all graph components

Phase 4: Basic Graph Algorithms

  • ✅ BFS (Breadth-First Search with predecessor tracking)
  • ✅ DFS (iterative Depth-First Search)
  • ✅ Topological Sort - Kahn's algorithm (in-degree based)
  • ✅ Topological Sort - DFS based (reverse postorder)
  • ✅ Cycle Detection (directed graphs via DFS)
  • ✅ Cycle Detection (undirected graphs via parent tracking)
  • ✅ Multi-source BFS (distance map from multiple sources)
  • ✅ 15+ comprehensive test cases

Phase 5: Shortest Path Algorithms

  • ✅ Dijkstra's algorithm (priority queue based)
  • ✅ A* pathfinding (with heuristic function support)
  • ✅ IDDFS (Iterative Deepening Depth-First Search)
  • ✅ DAG Shortest Path (topological sort based)
  • ✅ Bellman-Ford (handles negative edge weights)
  • ✅ Floyd-Warshall (all-pairs shortest paths)
  • ✅ 12+ comprehensive test cases
  • ⏳ Yen's K-Shortest Paths (deferred to future enhancement)

Phase 6: Graph Connectivity & Spanning Trees

  • ✅ SCC Tarjan (Strongly Connected Components)
  • ✅ Articulation Points (critical vertices)
  • ✅ Bridges (critical edges)
  • ✅ MST Kruskal (Minimum Spanning Tree)
  • ✅ MST Prim (alternative MST algorithm)
  • ✅ Union-Find data structure (with path compression)
  • ✅ 20+ comprehensive test cases

Phase 7: Flow & Matching Algorithms

  • ✅ Edmonds-Karp (BFS-based max flow)
  • ✅ Dinic's Algorithm (level graph with blocking flows)
  • ✅ Hopcroft-Karp (bipartite matching)

Phase 8: Centrality & Advanced Metrics

Phase 9: Caching & Probabilistic Structures

  • ✅ 20+ comprehensive test cases

Phase 10: String Search Algorithms

  • ✅ KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt pattern matching)
  • ✅ Rabin-Karp (rolling hash-based search)
  • ✅ Boyer-Moore (bad character heuristic)
  • ✅ O(n+m) time complexity for KMP
  • ✅ Multiple occurrence detection
  • ✅ 25+ comprehensive test cases
  • ✅ Algorithm parity verification

Phase 11: DOT Format Support

  • ✅ DOT parser (unmarshal from text)
  • ✅ DOT serializer (marshal to canonical format)
  • ✅ Support for graph and digraph
  • ✅ Node and edge attribute parsing
  • ✅ Strict mode with edge deduplication
  • ✅ Canonical ordering for deterministic output
  • ✅ Roundtrip parse/serialize compatibility
  • ✅ 15+ comprehensive test cases

Phase 12: GQL Emission

  • ✅ ISO-GQL CREATE clause generation
  • ✅ MATCH query for shortest path
  • ✅ Deterministic vertex/edge ordering
  • ✅ Parameter binding for query safety
  • ✅ ID sanitization for aliases
  • ✅ Support for directed/undirected graphs
  • ✅ 20+ comprehensive test cases

Phase 13: Fuzzing & Advanced Testing

  • ✅ Property-based tests for DOT roundtrip
  • ✅ BFS validity tests (no self-predecessors)
  • ✅ Dijkstra non-negative cost verification
  • ✅ Topological sort DAG validation
  • ✅ MST algorithm consistency (Kruskal vs Prim)
  • ✅ Bloom filter false negative prevention
  • ✅ String search algorithm agreement (KMP vs Rabin-Karp)
  • ✅ Union-Find idempotence verification
  • ✅ GQL emission determinism tests

  • ✅ Comprehensive performance guide (PERFORMANCE.md)
